design_detail: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis (DerSimonian-Laird; meta-regression with cluster-robust variance) of double- or triple-blind randomized placebo-controlled trials (parallel or crossover) of methylphenidate products approved or under FDA consideration in children and adolescents aged 6 to 18 with ADHD, conducted in clinical or naturalistic settings and reporting sleep-related adverse events, either spontaneously reported (coded to MedDRA terms) or elicited with rating scales. 35 trials gave 75 observations; pooled relative risks by MedDRA sleep category, meta-regressions of design and sample features, an ad hoc adjustment of each product's relative risk for confounders, and a model predicting the relative risk from the placebo adverse-event rate. Funded by a manufacturer of one of the compared products.
can_establish: How much more often sleep-related adverse events (insomnia and its subtypes, 'sleep disorder') were recorded with methylphenidate than with placebo in blinded trials in young people with ADHD up to August 2017, and which trial features go with larger or smaller relative risks.
cannot_establish: How many children per 100 had sleep problems on methylphenidate or placebo (absolute rates are not reported in the text); the effect on sleep measured objectively; effects in adults or with non-prescribed use; the trustworthiness of each trial (not appraised); and fair comparisons between products, given the funder's stake and a non-standard adjustment method.

sample.recruitment: Trials found in PubMed, Ovid (PsycInfo, EMBASE, Medline) and Web of Knowledge from inception to 18 August 2017, plus ClinicalTrials.gov, FDA medical reviews and labels, and reference lists; English only.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: double- or triple-blind randomized placebo-controlled trials, parallel or crossover; children or adolescents 6 to 18 with DSM-III or later ADHD or ICD-9 or later hyperkinetic disorder; methylphenidate products approved or under FDA consideration; clinical or naturalistic setting; sleep reported as spontaneous or elicited adverse events; English. Two studies using a global sleep rating that could not be coded were excluded.
sample.demographics: Not tabulated in the main text (covariates such as mean age, percentage male and percentage of Caucasian participants were extracted for meta-regression; details in supplementary tables not read).
sample.attrition: Not reported at review level; many screened studies lacked usable data (authors' limitations).
sample.selection_effects: Industry-dominated trial literature of approved products in young people with ADHD; English only; trials enrolling stimulant responders had lower relative risks, and many trials enrolled people previously treated with stimulants, which selects against those who stopped because of side effects.

exposure.measurement: Randomized methylphenidate products against placebo under double or triple blinding.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as described by the review: immediate-release methylphenidate and several extended or delayed-release products (osmotic-release oral system, transdermal system, delayed-release and extended-release HLD200, multilayer-release beads, PRC-063, extended-release dexmethylphenidate, long-acting, CD and sustained-release forms), dosed once, twice or three times a day, with dose strategies classified by prior stabilization or optimization and forced titration; no doses are given in the text. Extended-release products had higher mean relative risks for sleep-related adverse events than immediate-release ones (4.8 against 1.9, p = 0.03), and once-daily products higher than twice-daily or three-times-daily ones (4.6 against 1.7 and 2.5); the authors attribute this to doses taken too late in the morning or to differences in how long products act, and treat these features as properties of the products, not confounders.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable (clinical trials of a prescribed medicine); exclusion for psychiatric comorbidity was extracted as a covariate.

comparison.controls: Placebo arms of the same blinded trials (2606 patients).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Sleep problems are common in untreated ADHD; the placebo arm's adverse-event rate stands in for baseline propensity, which the review shows strongly predicts the relative risk.

outcomes.instruments: Spontaneously reported adverse events coded to MedDRA or COSTART terms (insomnia, initial, middle and terminal insomnia, combined insomnia, early morning awakening recoded as terminal insomnia, sleep disorder), or elicited by rating scales or questionnaires using clinical cut-points coded to the same categories plus sleep duration.
outcomes.validity_norms: Adverse-event recording depends on how it was elicited; the authors show that design features and the placebo rate shape the relative risk.
outcomes.operationalization: A sleep-related adverse event as a recorded MedDRA-coded complaint or a rating above a clinical cut-point; no objective sleep measure.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (six sleep categories pooled, plus many meta-regressions).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The trials were double- or triple-blind by inclusion; the review did not assess blinding integrity or other risk-of-bias domains.

analysis.effect_sizes: Pooled relative risks, methylphenidate against placebo: insomnia RR 1.61 (z = 9.2, p < 0.001); initial insomnia 2.78 (z = 6.6, p < 0.001); middle insomnia 2.97 (z printed as 183, p < 0.001); combined insomnia 2.97 (z = 6.4, p < 0.001); sleep disorder 1.99 (z = 4.2, p < 0.001). No confidence intervals, heterogeneity statistics or absolute rates are given in the text. Editors' calculation of 95% CIs from RR and z (assuming z = ln RR / SE): insomnia 1.45 to 1.78; initial insomnia 2.05 to 3.77; combined insomnia 2.13 to 4.15; sleep disorder 1.44 to 2.74; middle insomnia not computable. Drug and placebo adverse-event rates correlated r = 0.89 (p < 0.0001); the placebo rate was associated with the relative risk (z = -3.3, p = 0.001) and with the product studied (chi2 = 21.0, p = 0.01).
analysis.covariates: Meta-regressions of mean age, percentage male, percentage stimulant responders, year, number of sites, dosing strategy, rater and rating-scale use, and placebo adverse-event rate; missing covariate values entered as a separate category.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned (page searched).
analysis.selective_reporting: Terminal insomnia appears in the Discussion as significantly associated with methylphenidate but has no pooled result in the Results; per-trial values are only in figures.
analysis.power: Not addressed; 35 trials and about 5700 patients give precise pooled relative risks, but per-product comparisons rest on few trials.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In blinded trials in young people with ADHD, recorded insomnia was about 1.6 times as frequent with methylphenidate as with placebo, and initial and combined insomnia about 2.8 to 3 times as frequent, with 'sleep disorder' about twice as frequent. Most individual trials' adjusted relative risks did not differ from 1, some were below 1, and the size of the relative risk depended strongly on how often the placebo group reported sleep problems and on design features.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and discussion say several types of insomnia, including terminal insomnia in the Discussion, are associated with methylphenidate and that products differ after adjustment. Gaps: (1) terminal insomnia has no reported pooled estimate; (2) no interval or absolute rate accompanies any pooled estimate, although the authors themselves warn that relative risks cannot be read without absolute risks; (3) the product comparison uses an unvalidated adjustment and was funded by the maker of a competing product, with its employees extracting data; (4) the trials were not appraised. The authors' central methodological point, that the placebo rate constrains the relative risk, is shown clearly.

timeline.event: Kidwell et al., meta-analysis of stimulant medicines and objectively and subjectively measured sleep in young people with ADHD (Pediatrics), in the library's reference list but not read for this card.
This meta-analysis of sleep-related adverse events in methylphenidate trials, the first on this question by the authors' account.

replication.where_it_stands: The sleep-related adverse-event signal for methylphenidate in young people with ADHD is consistent at the pooled level; its size in absolute terms, its objective counterpart and any product differences remain to be read from other sources (for example kidwell_2015).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: items 8 and 10 can be judged only from a supplement that was not read; they are non-critical and cannot change the rating. Five critical items are 'no' (2: no protocol; 7: no excluded-study list; 9: no appraisal of the trials; 11: pooled estimates without intervals or heterogeneity and non-independent observations; 13: risk of bias not considered, which follows from 9), while 4 is partly met and 15 met, which under AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence. The review may be cited for the direction and approximate size of the pooled relative risks of recorded sleep complaints in blinded trials in young people with ADHD (with the editors' intervals labelled as such) and for its demonstration that the placebo rate constrains the relative risk; not for comparisons between products, given the funder's stake.

design_detail: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of studies that randomly assigned children and adolescents with ADHD to stimulant conditions and measured sleep by actigraphy or polysomnography: 9 studies, 246 young people; methylphenidate in 6 (Corkum, Galland, Gruber, Sangal, Schwartz, Tirosh) and amphetamine-class medicines in 3 (Chatoor; Giblin & Strobel, lisdexamfetamine; Santisteban, mixed amphetamine salts). Hedges' g compared baseline nights (or, in 4 studies, placebo nights) with medicated nights for sleep latency, sleep efficiency and total sleep time; trim-and-fill for publication bias; study-level moderator regressions. CINAHL, PsycINFO and PubMed searched from February 2014 to March 2015.
can_establish: The average direction and standardized size of differences in objectively measured sleep onset, efficiency and duration between medicated and unmedicated nights in small published studies of young people with ADHD.
cannot_establish: Differences in minutes (only standardized effects are given), the randomized effect against placebo (most comparisons use pre-treatment nights), effects in adults or with non-prescribed use, adaptation within children over time (the duration moderator compares 7 studies), or the trials' risk of bias (coded but not reported).

sample.recruitment: 9927 records screened, 167 full texts examined, 158 excluded (list in the supplement, not read), 9 included (p. 5).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Children or adolescents diagnosed with ADHD, random assignment to stimulant conditions, sleep measured by actigraphy or polysomnography; excluded if key statistics were unavailable after contacting authors; no restriction on country or year (p. 2).
sample.demographics: Mean ages 102 to 139 months (about 8.5 to 11.6 years); 41.7% to 85.3% boys; 7 to 50 participants per study (Table 1, p. 4).
sample.selection_effects: Published studies only. One included study is titled a matched case-control study (Galland et al., 2010) despite the randomization criterion. Schwartz et al. (2004) and Gruber et al. (2006) come from the same group and share a mean age of 110.4 months, so their samples may overlap (editors' observation; not addressed by the review).

exposure.measurement: Assigned stimulant condition in each study (Table 1).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions (Table 1): 2 to 49 days on medication; mean total daily dose 15.6 to 48.75 mg where reported; 1 to 3 doses a day; short-, medium- and long-acting forms; oral. One condition per study was used (mixed amphetamine salts in Santisteban et al.; the low-dose condition in Corkum et al.) (pp. 2-3).

comparison.controls: Each child's own unmedicated baseline sleep, or placebo nights in the 4 studies that did not report baseline (p. 3).

outcomes.instruments: Actigraphy in most studies; polysomnography in Chatoor et al. and Galland et al. (and in Giblin & Strobel for latency, by Table 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: Polysomnography described as the gold standard; it showed larger efficiency effects than actigraphy (p. 7).
outcomes.operationalization: Sleep latency, sleep efficiency and total sleep time; other sleep variables too sparsely reported (p. 3).

analysis.effect_sizes: Hedges' g, random effects: sleep latency 0.78 (95% CI 0.54 to 1.02), Q(6) = 18.35, I2 67.30%; trim-and-fill (3 studies imputed) 0.54 (0.28 to 0.81). Sleep efficiency -0.39 (-0.69 to -0.08), I2 83.37%; trim-and-fill (1 imputed) -0.32 (-0.63 to -0.01). Total sleep time -0.59 (-0.84 to -0.35), I2 82.67%, no asymmetry. Moderators (study level): latency effect larger with more doses a day (b = 0.42 per extra dose, k = 5, p = .001); efficiency effect smaller with more days on medication (b = 0.05 per day, k = 7) and more nights recorded (0.04 per night), larger with polysomnography (-0.81) and with a higher share of boys (-0.02 per percentage point); no moderators for total sleep time. Single studies: latency 0.44 to 1.15; efficiency -1.76 to 0.48; total sleep -1.31 to -0.16 (Table 1).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable (moderator regressions one at a time).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration mentioned; PRISMA followed.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only three of the coded sleep variables were analysed because others were too sparsely reported.
analysis.power: Seven studies per outcome; moderator analyses with 4 to 7 studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 9 small studies, medicated nights showed longer sleep onset (g 0.78; 0.54 after trim-and-fill), lower sleep efficiency (-0.39) and shorter sleep (-0.59) than unmedicated, mostly pre-treatment, nights, with high heterogeneity.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusions say that stimulant medications “impair the sleep of children and adolescents” (p. 9), and the review stresses that it included only randomized trials. Gaps: (1) the effect sizes mostly compare medicated nights with pre-treatment nights, not the randomized placebo contrast, so the strength of randomization does not carry over to the estimates; (2) the trials' risk of bias was coded but neither reported nor used; (3) the dose-frequency and duration moderators come from 5 to 7 studies but are offered as guidance for prescribing; (4) no difference in minutes is given.

timeline.event: Cortese et al., meta-analysis of subjective and objective sleep in children with ADHD (cited as background, ref. 7).
This meta-analysis of objectively measured sleep on stimulants.
Faraone et al., meta-analysis of sleep-related adverse events in placebo-controlled methylphenidate trials; a different outcome (reported events) from a partly overlapping literature.

replication.where_it_stands: The objective-sleep counterpart of the adverse-event meta-analyses; both point the same way, but the literatures overlap, so they are not fully independent. A meta-analysis of the placebo contrasts with sleep in minutes is still missing.

funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no financial relationships or conflicts of interest (p. 9).
funding.affiliations_note: University of Nebraska-Lincoln. Four of the nine included studies were coded as funded by a pharmaceutical company (Table 1; Gruber et al. is coded both ways).

what_would_settle_it: An individual-participant-data meta-analysis of placebo-controlled randomized trials with actigraphy or polysomnography, reporting minutes of sleep onset and total sleep by formulation and by weeks since starting, with repeated measurement over months.

design_detail: Two-phase clinical study in a hospital ADHD programme in Vancouver: 10 nights of baseline, then sleep-hygiene instruction for all children (an uncontrolled before-after phase), then, for those whose insomnia persisted, a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial of melatonin (two 10-day periods, each followed by 5 days of placebo washout), then 90 days of open-label melatonin for responders (Figure 1, p. 515). Sleep from parent sleep diaries (somnologs) and wrist actigraphy. The card's design and risk-of-bias rating refer to the randomized phase.
can_establish: Within the randomized phase, whether melatonin shortened the time to fall asleep compared with placebo in children with ADHD on stimulant medicine whose initial insomnia persisted after a sleep-hygiene run-in.
cannot_establish: The effect of sleep hygiene itself (no control group), the effect of melatonin without prior sleep hygiene, in children not taking stimulants or with other sleep disorders (excluded; no polysomnography), long-term effects under blinding (the 90-day phase was open-label and limited to responders), or daytime effects beyond a clinician's global rating and a parent ADHD scale.

sample.recruitment: Clinical referrals to the Provincial ADHD Program, British Columbia Children's Hospital (pp. 514-515).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age 6 to 14; ADHD (DISC-IV, Child Symptom Inventories, confirmed by a clinician); stimulant dose unchanged for at least 2 months; mean sleep-onset latency over 60 minutes on 10 nights of parent diaries; parents able to keep diaries; child able to wear an actigraph and accept a fixed bedtime. Excluded: stressful circumstances, bed-sharing or other environmental causes, medical or psychiatric illness linked to insomnia or needing other sedating or activating medicines, several households unless all caregivers could take part, known major sleep disorders (not screened by polysomnography) (p. 514).
sample.demographics: 90.9% boys; mean age 10.29 (6.5 to 14.7); 87.9% white; 67% on methylphenidate (a third OROS) and 30% on dextroamphetamine; 54% with oppositional disorder, 12% enuresis; sleep problem rated mild in 3.0%, moderate 42.4%, marked 30.3% and severe 24.2% (p. 516).
sample.attrition: Five of 33 withdrew before randomization; of 23 eligible, 1 withdrew and 3 were discontinued for protocol violations, leaving 19 analysed per protocol; the authors say results did not differ materially when the others were included (p. 515).
sample.selection_effects: Motivated families able to follow the programme; children who responded to sleep hygiene were removed before randomization, so the trial sample was enriched for persisting insomnia.

exposure.measurement: Pharmacy-dispensed blister cards; at least 80% adherence required in each phase (p. 515).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: short-acting pharmaceutical-grade melatonin 5 mg made by the sponsor, taken 20 minutes before bedtime, for 10 days per period (p. 515). Sleep hygiene: a consistent bedtime and waking time with a target of at least 9.5 hours in bed within age norms, no caffeine and no naps, reviewed with parents from 10 nights of diaries (p. 514).
exposure.polysubstance: All children took stimulants at stable doses; other medicines and natural products were monitored (p. 515).

comparison.controls: Placebo in the crossover, each child serving as his or her own control; for the sleep-hygiene phase, the child's own baseline.
comparison.matching: Within-person; order randomized in blocks of four by the pharmacy (p. 514).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Undiagnosed primary sleep disorders were possible, since no polysomnography was done (p. 517).

outcomes.instruments: Parent-completed somnolog (parents checked every 15 minutes whether the child was asleep); wrist actigraph with proprietary software; Clinical Global Impression-Improvement; Conners ADHD scale, parent version (CADS-P); adverse events (p. 515).
outcomes.validity_norms: Actigraphy reliability cited; diary and actigraph sleep-onset latencies correlated r = 0.76 after sleep hygiene (p. 516).
outcomes.operationalization: Primary: mean sleep-onset latency (time from being put to bed to falling asleep) in each phase, from the diaries; secondary: night-to-night variability, total sleep, actigraph measures, responders (much or very much improved), ADHD symptoms.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Children, parents and staff were blind to treatment order in the randomized phase; the sleep-hygiene and open-label phases were unblinded.

analysis.effect_sizes: Sleep hygiene (before-after, no control): diary latency 91.7 to 69.3 minutes (t(28) = 2.77, p = .01) and actigraph 98.1 to 73.0 (t(21) = 2.92, p < .01); effect size 0.67; diary variability 47.7 to 29.1 minutes (t(28) = 3.81, p < .01); 5 responders (latency under 60 minutes); 21% rated much or very much improved. Melatonin against placebo: diary latency 46.4 (SD 26.4) against 62.1 (SD 26.6) minutes, t(20) = -3.06, p < .01, with a significant period effect, t(20) = -2.20, p < .05, and no carryover; effect size 0.6; actigraph latency t(18) = -4.54, p < .01; diary total sleep 15.0 minutes longer, t(20) = 3.13, p < .01; actigraph total sleep and variability not different; clinician ratings and CADS-P not different. Open label (responders only): latency 31 minutes, sleep duration 23 minutes longer (t(12) = 3.90, p < .01). Baseline to end of open label: 91 to 31 minutes, effect size 1.7. Adverse events: 20% of all events during melatonin and 23% during placebo; one severe migraine; rash from the actigraph band in two (pp. 516-517).
analysis.covariates: Period adjusted for in the crossover analysis (Senn).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or published protocol is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Actigraph latency means for the randomized phase are not given; the text attaches the 16-minute difference to the actigraph, while the diary means differ by 15.7 minutes.
analysis.power: Planned to detect a 30-minute change with 25 children (80% power, 20% dropout allowed); 19 were analysed and the observed difference was about 16 minutes (p. 515).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Melatonin shortened parent-recorded time to fall asleep by about 16 minutes against placebo (effect size 0.6) in about 20 children, with a concordant actigraph result, no difference in clinicians' global ratings or ADHD symptoms, and mild adverse events as frequent as on placebo; sleep hygiene was followed by an uncontrolled improvement of about 22 to 25 minutes.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that combined sleep hygiene and melatonin was “a safe and effective treatment for initial insomnia” (p. 512), citing a combined effect size of 1.7 and a 60-minute fall. Gaps: (1) the 1.7 and the 60 minutes are uncontrolled before-after figures at the end of open-label treatment in the 17 children chosen as melatonin responders; (2) safety rests on 10 days of blinded melatonin in about 20 children; (3) the sleep-hygiene effect has no control group; (4) clinicians' ratings of improvement did not differ between melatonin and placebo.

timeline.event: Weiss et al., pilot crossover trial in 9 children with ADHD (as described, p. 514).
Tjon Pian Gi et al., open-label study of melatonin in 24 children with ADHD (as described, p. 514).

replication.where_it_stands: One small sponsor-funded crossover trial; other trials of melatonin in children with ADHD (not read here) should be read before any stronger statement.

funding.funder: Investigator-initiated trial sponsored by Circa Dia BV, which made the melatonin (pp. 512, 515).
funding.declared_conflicts: First author: consultant, advisory board or speaker's bureau member, or holder of research contracts or grants with Eli Lilly, Shire, Janssen Ortho, Novartis, Purdue, Johnson & Johnson and Circa Dia; the other authors none (p. 518).
funding.affiliations_note: University of British Columbia; Provincial ADHD Program; British Columbia Children's Hospital.

what_would_settle_it: A registered, adequately powered parallel-group trial of melatonin against placebo in children with ADHD and stimulant-related insomnia, with and without sleep hygiene in a factorial design, analysed by intention to treat, with diaries, actigraphy and daytime outcomes and blinded follow-up over months.

design_detail: Systematic review and frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42014008976; protocol published) of double-blind randomized trials lasting at least 1 week of oral ADHD medicines given alone (amphetamines including lisdexamfetamine, atomoxetine, bupropion, clonidine, guanfacine, methylphenidate including dexmethylphenidate, modafinil) against each other or placebo, analysed separately for children and adolescents (5 to 17 years) and for adults. Primary outcomes at the time closest to 12 weeks: clinician-rated change in core ADHD symptoms (in children and adolescents also teacher-rated) and dropouts because of side effects. 133 trials (81 in children and adolescents, 51 in adults, 1 in both). The PDF read is the online-first version (PDF pp. 1–12).
can_establish: Average short-term (about 12 weeks) differences in clinician-rated core ADHD symptoms and in stopping a trial because of side effects for each class of medicine against placebo and, mostly through indirect comparison, between classes, in double-blind trials up to April 2017.
cannot_establish: Long-term benefit or harm (too few trials beyond 12 weeks); the absolute numbers of people who benefit or stop (the article gives only odds ratios and standardized differences); rare harms such as psychosis (not studied); differences between products within a class or by dose; a trial-based head-to-head comparison of amphetamines with methylphenidate in adults (none in the network); effects in people whose other conditions need other medicines (excluded).

sample.recruitment: Searches of PubMed, BIOSIS Previews, CINAHL, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Embase, ERIC, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, OpenGrey, Web of Science Core Collection, ProQuest Dissertations and Theses (UK and Ireland; abstracts and international) and the WHO International Trials Registry Platform including ClinicalTrials.gov, from inception to 7 April 2017, without language restriction; FDA, EMA and manufacturers' websites and the references of reviews and guidelines hand-searched; study authors and manufacturers contacted for unpublished data (PDF p. 3). 9948 records screened and 3525 full texts assessed (Figure 1, PDF p. 3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Double-blind randomized trials (parallel, crossover or cluster) of at least 1 week in children (5 to 11 years), adolescents (12 to 17) or adults with a primary DSM or ICD diagnosis of ADHD; no restriction by subtype, sex, IQ, socioeconomic status or comorbidity except comorbidities needing other medicines; oral monotherapy compared with another drug or placebo. Enrichment designs (only responders kept after a run-in) were excluded because they may inflate efficacy and tolerability (PDF p. 3). The primary analysis was limited to doses within the therapeutic range, per FDA recommendations where applicable (PDF p. 4), and trials using doses above guideline recommendations were excluded (PDF p. 9).
sample.demographics: Not given in the article; the characteristics of the included trials are in the appendix (pp. 283–381), which was not read.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; leaving a trial because of side effects (tolerability) or for any reason (acceptability) are outcomes.
sample.selection_effects: Only double-blind trials, mostly placebo-controlled and short. Enrichment designs, doses above guidelines, combination therapy and, according to the note to Figure 1, trials including patients with comorbid disorders were excluded (PDF pp. 3, 9). Industry sponsorship of the trials could not be analysed (PDF p. 8). The search ended in April 2017; three eligible trials found in May 2018 were not added (PDF p. 9). Unpublished data were used for 83% of trials (PDF p. 4).

exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Oral; within FDA-licensed or guideline ranges in the primary analysis. Two dose sensitivity analyses (trials at FDA-licensed doses only; guideline ranges differing from FDA recommendations) confirmed the primary analysis (PDF pp. 4, 8). Doses by product are not shown in the article; lisdexamfetamine was separated from the other amphetamines in a post hoc analysis.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable; trials of single medicines only, combination therapy excluded.

comparison.controls: Placebo or another active medicine within trials; network estimates combine direct and indirect evidence. In children and adolescents some trials compared amphetamines with methylphenidate directly; in adults the network has no direct amphetamine–methylphenidate link, both being connected only to placebo (Figure 2, PDF p. 4).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable within trials. The network assumes transitivity, which the authors defend by saying that participants' previous exposure and response to ADHD medicines were evenly distributed across trials and nodes (PDF p. 9).

outcomes.instruments: Validated rating scales measuring only core ADHD symptoms (list in appendix pp. 273–274, not read), rated by clinicians, teachers, parents or adults themselves; Clinical Global Impression–Improvement (CGI-I); proportion leaving because of any side effect (tolerability) and for any reason (acceptability); change in weight and blood pressure (PDF p. 3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Only validated scales measuring core symptoms were included (PDF pp. 9–10). Risk of bias of trials assessed with the Cochrane tool; certainty with GRADE for network meta-analyses (PDF p. 3).
outcomes.operationalization: Efficacy: standardized mean difference (Hedges' g) in symptom change; tolerability and acceptability: odds ratios. In Table 1 negative values favour the drug in the row; in Table 2 odds ratios above 1 favour the drug in the column (PDF pp. 6–7).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (3 primary and 6 secondary outcomes, two age groups, every pairwise comparison).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level; the included trials were double-blind. Data were extracted by at least two independent investigators (PDF p. 3).

analysis.effect_sizes: Network estimates at about 12 weeks (certainty by GRADE). Clinician-rated symptoms against placebo: amphetamines SMD −1.02 (95% CI −1.19 to −0.85) in children and adolescents and −0.79 (−0.99 to −0.58) in adults; methylphenidate −0.78 (−0.93 to −0.62) and −0.49 (−0.64 to −0.35); all four moderate. Amphetamines against methylphenidate: −0.24 (−0.44 to −0.05) in children and adolescents and −0.29 (−0.54 to −0.05) in adults, both low. Teacher ratings in children and adolescents: methylphenidate −0.82 (−1.16 to −0.48, low) against placebo; no data for amphetamines. Dropouts because of side effects against placebo: amphetamines OR 2.30 (1.36 to 3.89) in children and adolescents and 3.26 (1.54 to 6.92) in adults (moderate); methylphenidate 1.44 (0.90 to 2.31, low) and 2.39 (1.40 to 4.08, high). Amphetamines against methylphenidate: OR 1.60 (0.94 to 2.73, low) in children and adolescents and 1.36 (0.54 to 3.43, very low) in adults. Acceptability against placebo: methylphenidate in children and adolescents OR 0.69 (0.52 to 0.91); amphetamines in adults 0.68 (0.49 to 0.95). Weight against placebo (SMD): amphetamines −0.71 (−1.15 to −0.27) and −0.60 (−1.03 to −0.18); methylphenidate −0.77 (−1.09 to −0.45) and −0.74 (−1.20 to −0.28). Systolic blood pressure: amphetamines in children and adolescents SMD 0.09 (0.01 to 0.18); methylphenidate in adults 0.17 (0.05 to 0.30). Diastolic: amphetamines 0.21 (0.12 to 0.31) and methylphenidate 0.24 (0.14 to 0.33) in the younger group (see reporting issues on the age group printed), methylphenidate 0.20 (0.08 to 0.32) in adults. Common heterogeneity SD in children and adolescents 0.355 (teacher ratings), 0.188 (clinician ratings) and 0.268 (tolerability); in adults 0.178 and 0.282; no significant global inconsistency. No absolute event rates are given in the article.
analysis.covariates: None at review level. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses for study length, comorbidities, IQ, crossover design, unfair dose comparisons and data imputation were reported as generally robust (appendix pp. 479–491, not read); gender, age (children against adolescents), low risk of bias, medication status and industry sponsorship could not be assessed for lack of data (PDF p. 8).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42014008976; protocol published (BMJ Open 2017, reference 30); PRISMA extension for network meta-analyses followed (PDF p. 3). Changes to the original protocol are listed in the appendix (p. 25, not read); the lisdexamfetamine analysis was post hoc; planned analyses at 26 and 52 weeks and several planned subgroups could not be done (PDF pp. 4, 8, 10).
analysis.selective_reporting: Many results are only in the appendix: the pairwise meta-analyses and their heterogeneity, the amphetamine-versus-methylphenidate CGI-I estimate (described in the Discussion as no significant difference, without numbers), parent and self ratings by drug pair, blood-pressure estimates between drugs, the dose analyses and the funnel plots.
analysis.power: Not applicable. The authors note that some nodes of the network included few trials and that actual head-to-head trials were few (PDF p. 9).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In trials of about 12 weeks, amphetamines and methylphenidate both reduced clinician-rated ADHD symptoms more than placebo in children, adolescents and adults, amphetamines by a slightly larger margin (SMD 0.24 to 0.29 more, low certainty, largely from indirect comparison); teacher ratings exist only for methylphenidate. Amphetamines led to more stopping because of side effects than placebo in both age groups and methylphenidate in adults only; the two did not differ significantly from each other in either age group. Both lowered weight and raised blood pressure slightly compared with placebo. There is no evidence beyond 12 weeks.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the efficacy differences favouring amphetamines head-to-head comparisons (PDF p. 1), but they are network estimates, and the authors themselves state that comparisons between drugs were frequently based on indirect evidence (PDF p. 9); in adults the network has no direct amphetamine–methylphenidate trials (Figure 2, PDF p. 4). The recommendation of methylphenidate as first choice in children and adolescents (abstract; PDF p. 9) rests on each drug's comparison with placebo for tolerability and acceptability (amphetamines worse than placebo, methylphenidate not), while the network estimate between the two drugs was not significant (OR 1.60, 0.94 to 2.73) and the Results state that no differences in tolerability were found between active drugs (PDF p. 7). The Interpretation correctly limits the conclusions to short-term treatment and calls for long-term research.

timeline.event: Protocol published (Cortese et al., BMJ Open; reference 30 of the review; not read)

Farhat et al., with authors in common, reused this review's original searches (to April 2017), updated them to January 2024 and analysed blood pressure, pulse and ECG measures by network meta-analysis

replication.where_it_stands: By its authors' account the most comprehensive synthesis of the short-term efficacy and tolerability of ADHD medicines up to its search date (PDF p. 8). Its search pool underlies Farhat et al. (2025), so the two are not independent evidence. For amphetamines against methylphenidate it gives a small, low-certainty efficacy advantage for amphetamines and no significant difference in stopping because of side effects.

domains.note: GRADE ratings, which include risk of bias, are given for every comparison in Tables 1 and 2 and discussed, with low or very low certainty for most indirect comparisons (PDF pp. 6–8, 10).

domains.domain: 14. Heterogeneity explained and discussed
domains.note: Common heterogeneity SDs reported and compared with empirical distributions, subgroup and sensitivity analyses run where data allowed, and heterogeneity discussed (PDF pp. 7–9); the authors' argument that heterogeneity increases external validity is a judgment rather than an analysis.

domains.domain: 15. Publication bias investigated (critical)
domains.note: The article states only that funnel plots are shown in the appendix (pp. 630–632); it reports neither their result nor a discussion of the likely impact of small-study or publication bias, and the limitations say only that missing information cannot be ruled out (PDF pp. 8–9).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding, the funder's role and the authors' interests are declared (PDF pp. 4, 10).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: One critical item is not met (15: no result or discussion of publication bias in the article), which by AMSTAR 2 gives low confidence; item 2 is partly met, items 4, 7, 9, 11 and 13 are met, item 12 is not met, and items 5, 8 and 10 can be judged only from the appendix. If the appendix reports and interprets the funnel plots, item 15 could become yes and the overall rating moderate. This rates the review's conduct as reported, not its value: the search, the systematic use of unpublished data and the GRADE ratings are strong. Cite for: short-term (about 12 weeks) estimates of efficacy and of stopping because of side effects for amphetamines and methylphenidate against placebo and against each other, with their certainty ratings. Do not cite for: long-term effects, absolute risks, rare harms, specific products or doses, or as head-to-head trial evidence in adults.

design_detail: Randomized, double-blind crossover trial of two active stimulants without a placebo condition, run within a trial of their relative efficacy whose efficacy results are not reported in this paper. 125 children aged 5 to 15 years with DSM-IV ADHD, referred to a hospital behaviour clinic in Melbourne, took dexamphetamine (DEX) 0.15 mg/kg per dose and methylphenidate (MPH) 0.3 mg/kg per dose twice daily for 2 weeks each in random order, with a 24-hour washout. Parents rated 17 listed complaints on Barkley's Side Effects Rating Scale (0 = absent, 1 to 9 = severity) before treatment and at the end of each fortnight. The amphetamine studied is dexamphetamine alone.
can_establish: Within the same children, at these two fixed doses given twice daily for two weeks each, how parent ratings of 17 listed complaints differed between dexamphetamine and methylphenidate under randomized order and double blinding, and how often each complaint was already reported before treatment.
cannot_establish: Whether either drug causes or relieves a complaint compared with a dummy pill (there was no placebo, so drug-versus-baseline contrasts are unblinded and mixed with time, expectation and regression to the mean); whether the two doses were equally effective (efficacy is not reported here beyond parents' global ratings), so a difference between the drugs may reflect the 1:2 dose ratio chosen; effects after two weeks, at other doses or schedules, in adolescents, adults or girls (11 of 125), or with non-medical use.

sample.recruitment: Clinic: ambulatory patients referred to the Royal Children's Hospital, Melbourne, for ADHD assessment by paediatricians, family practitioners, school nurses or psychologists, or by parents themselves; enrolled April 1995 to August 1996 (p. 663).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age 5 to 15 years; DSM-IV ADHD on the DuPaul rating scale (a symptom counted only if rated often or very often); T score at least 1.5 SD above the mean on the Attention Problems scale of the Child Behavior Checklist or Teacher Report Form; no intellectual disability, gross neurological abnormality or Tourette's syndrome; a clinical decision to try stimulant medicine (p. 663).
sample.demographics: 114 boys and 11 girls; mean age 104.8 months (SD 27.6; range 60 to 179), about 8.7 years (editors' conversion); mean estimated IQ 98.9 (SD 13.8); 101 of mixed type (printed as 81.8%; see reporting issues), 22 (17.6%) predominantly inattentive, 2 (1.6%) predominantly hyperactive-impulsive; mean Child Behavior Checklist attention-problems T score 75.9 (SD 8.4) (p. 663).
sample.attrition: Four children (3.2%) stopped one trial period because of severe adverse effects, two on each drug (p. 664). How their ratings for that period were handled is not stated; the degrees of freedom of the F tests (2, 122) imply 124 children in the analyses (editors' inference; see reporting issues).
sample.selection_effects: Referred clinic sample in whom treatment had already been decided, 91% boys, mostly of primary-school age; prior stimulant treatment is not reported. Parents who had sought an ADHD assessment made all the ratings, and the authors suggest some may have over-reported symptoms at baseline (p. 664). One hospital in one country.

exposure.measurement: Assigned by the investigators: both drugs as crushed powder in identical opaque gelatin capsules (p. 663); adherence was not measured or reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: dexamphetamine 0.15 mg/kg per dose and methylphenidate 0.3 mg/kg per dose, rounded to the nearest capsule size (2.5 and 5 mg capsules for DEX, 5 and 10 mg for MPH), by mouth twice a day after breakfast and after lunch, for 2 weeks each with a 24-hour washout between (p. 663). The authors call the doses moderate and note that other doses and spacing might give different side-effect profiles (p. 666).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable (children). Other medicines are not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Baseline ratings were made before any trial medicine; drug ratings at the end of each 2-week period while it was being taken.

comparison.controls: Within-person: each child on the other drug (randomized order), and the same child's pre-treatment baseline. No placebo condition.
comparison.matching: Self-controlled crossover; order and period effects are not reported.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not an issue for the dexamphetamine-versus-methylphenidate contrast (within-person, randomized order). For contrasts with baseline, change over time, parents' expectations and changed perception of the child, and regression to the mean cannot be separated from drug effects; the authors raise the first two possibilities themselves (p. 664).

outcomes.instruments: Barkley's Side Effects Rating Scale (SERS), presented to parents as a behavior questionnaire to disguise its purpose: 17 items (trouble sleeping, poor appetite, irritability, proneness to crying, anxiousness, sadness/unhappiness, headaches, stomachaches, nightmares, daydreams, talking little with others, uninterested in others, drowsiness, biting fingernails, unusually happy, dizziness, tics or nervous movements), each scored 0 (absent) or 1 to 9 (severity), completed by parents at baseline and at the end of each fortnight (pp. 663–664). Efficacy measures were collected (Conners teacher and parent scales, Continuous Performance Test, parents' global ratings) but are not reported except parents' global improvement (p. 663).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors state that no normative data have been published for the SERS and that no normed questionnaire for stimulant side effects exists (p. 663).
outcomes.operationalization: A genuine side effect: a complaint both more frequent (McNemar test) and more severe (repeated-measures ANOVA) on a drug than at baseline (p. 665, Discussion, 8th paragraph). Drug comparison: dexamphetamine-versus-methylphenidate contrasts on the number of complaints, their mean severity and the severity of each item.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Partial: the significance level was set at 0.01 because of the number of comparisons (p. 663); no formal correction across 36 measures (2 summary measures, 17 prevalence and 17 severity items) with up to 3 pairwise contrasts each.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Investigators, families, children and teachers were blind to the order throughout (p. 663). Baseline ratings were made off medication and could not be blinded. Blinding was not checked.

analysis.effect_sizes: Number of complaints (Table 1, p. 664): baseline 8.19 (SD 3.97), DEX 7.64 (3.83), MPH 7.19 (3.82); F(2,122) = 3.72, p = .03; only baseline versus MPH significant at p < .01. Mean severity of the complaints reported: 4.08 (1.56), 3.73 (1.68), 3.24 (1.46); F = 15.98, p < .01; baseline versus MPH and DEX versus MPH significant. Editors' calculation: DEX minus MPH mean severity 0.49 points on the 1-to-9 scale, about 0.31 of the pooled SD (ignoring the within-child correlation, which the paper does not give). Prevalence (Table 2, p. 664): poor appetite 43 (34%) at baseline, 74 (59%) on DEX, 69 (56%) on MPH; trouble sleeping 67 (54%), 88 (70%), 79 (64%). Item severity means (Table 3, p. 665; no SDs printed), baseline, DEX, MPH: trouble sleeping 2.21, 3.61, 2.69; poor appetite 1.22, 2.74, 2.12; irritability 4.57, 3.65, 2.94; proneness to crying 3.35, 3.4, 2.7; anxiousness 3.94, 2.71, 2.07; sadness/unhappiness 2.86, 2.43, 1.69; nightmares 1.09, .79, .48. Item means below 1 show that Table 3 averages include children without the complaint, scored 0 (editors' inference).
analysis.covariates: None. Repeated-measures ANOVA (Hotelling's multivariate test) with planned pairwise contrasts, and McNemar tests for prevalence (pp. 663–664); period and order effects were not analysed or reported.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned (trial run 1995–1996).
analysis.selective_reporting: The efficacy results of the same trial are not reported here (p. 663). Table 3 gives no SDs or confidence intervals; prevalence contrasts between DEX and MPH are not shown (Table 2 marks only contrasts with baseline); period and carryover effects are not reported.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Parents already reported many of the 17 listed complaints before treatment (for example irritability in 82% and anxiousness in 77% of children). Compared with baseline, poor appetite was more frequent and more severe on both drugs, and trouble sleeping on dexamphetamine; most other complaints were reported less often or as less severe on the drugs. Dexamphetamine was rated more severe than methylphenidate overall (mean severity 3.73 vs 3.24) and on six items, mostly emotional ones, while the number of complaints did not differ between the drugs. Ratings were mostly in the mild part of the 0-to-9 scale, and four children stopped a period because of severe effects, two on each drug.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that both drugs caused appetite suppression, that dexamphetamine caused insomnia, and that many symptoms attributed to stimulants are pre-existing characteristics that improve with stimulant treatment (p. 662). The causal statements rest on unblinded comparisons with baseline, although the authors note that comparing with baseline may if anything understate side effects (p. 665). Improvement with treatment cannot be separated from placebo or time effects in a trial without a placebo, and the Discussion itself offers parental over-reporting before diagnosis and mothers' changed perception of the child as alternative explanations (p. 664). The comparison of the two drugs is randomized and blind but at one fixed dose ratio without shown equal efficacy, which the authors acknowledge (p. 666). The Discussion's statement that only trouble sleeping and irritability averaged above 3 on DEX overlooks proneness to crying (3.4 in Table 3) (p. 665).

timeline.event: Conners randomly assigned 75 children with minimal brain dysfunction to methylphenidate 30 mg, dexamphetamine 15 mg or placebo for 6 weeks: dexamphetamine produced significantly more side effects than methylphenidate, few of them moderate or severe (as summarized by Efron et al., p. 665; not read)

Pelham et al., random-order double-blind crossover in 22 boys: sustained-release dexamphetamine gave more adverse effects than the other preparations, not significantly, and severity was not reported (as summarized by Efron et al., pp. 665–666; not read)

Elia et al., crossover of methylphenidate and dexamphetamine at various doses in 48 boys: 83% had some side effects on both; decreased appetite 85% vs 95%, sleep difficulties 79% vs 81% (as summarized by Efron et al., p. 666; not read)
This trial: 125 children; dexamphetamine rated more severe than methylphenidate overall and on six items, with the same number of complaints

Network meta-analysis of double-blind trials: stopping because of side effects did not differ significantly between amphetamines and methylphenidate in children and adolescents (OR 1.60, 0.94 to 2.73, low certainty); its main text does not list its trials, so whether it includes this one is not known from the article

replication.where_it_stands: By its authors' account the largest direct comparison of the two drugs' side effects at the time (p. 666), in one clinic, at one dose ratio, for two weeks each, with parent ratings on a scale without norms. The network meta-analysis of Cortese et al. (2018) found no significant difference between amphetamines and methylphenidate in stopping because of side effects in children and adolescents; that outcome differs from rated severity, so it neither confirms nor contradicts this trial.

what_would_settle_it: A double-blind trial with a placebo condition comparing an amphetamine and methylphenidate at doses titrated to equal benefit, over months rather than two weeks, with a validated side-effect measure, absolute rates of each complaint and of stopping, and enough girls, adolescents and adults to describe them.

domains.domain: Randomization process
domains.note: Children were randomized to which drug came first (p. 663), but sequence generation and allocation concealment are not described and baseline characteristics by order are not reported.

domains.domain: Bias arising from period and carryover effects (crossover)
domains.note: A 24-hour washout between two 2-week periods, with ratings at the end of each period, makes carryover unlikely to dominate, but period and order effects were neither analysed nor reported.

domains.domain: Deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Identical capsules and blinding of everyone involved (p. 663), but the blind was not checked and distinctive effects such as insomnia could reveal the drug; four children stopped a period early and how they were analysed is not stated.

domains.domain: Missing outcome data
domains.note: The degrees of freedom imply 124 of 125 children in the analyses; who is missing, and what was recorded for the periods stopped early, is not stated.

domains.domain: Measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Parent ratings on a questionnaire without norms (p. 663), made blind for the comparison of the two drugs. The baseline rating was made off medication and unblinded, so for contrasts with baseline this domain would be high.

domains.domain: Selection of the reported result
domains.note: No protocol or registration; all 17 items are tabulated, but between-drug prevalence contrasts, per-item SDs and the efficacy results of the trial are not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: RoB 2 applies to the randomized comparison of dexamphetamine with methylphenidate, which is within-person and double-blind with identical capsules, with all 17 items reported. The concerns are undescribed randomization and missing-data handling, unexamined period effects, an untested blind and a parent-rated scale without norms; they are concerns of reporting more than of a likely direction of bias, so the overall judgment stays at some concerns rather than high. The contrasts of each drug with baseline are not randomized comparisons: without a placebo they are at high risk of bias and should not be cited as effects of the drugs. Cite for: at the study's doses (DEX 0.15 mg/kg and MPH 0.3 mg/kg twice daily) for two weeks each, parents rated dexamphetamine's complaints as somewhat more severe, mostly sleep and emotional items, with the same number of complaints and the same small number of children stopping. Do not cite for: effects against placebo, other doses, long-term use, adolescents or adults, or a comparison of strength between the drugs.

key_findings.finding: Design as conducted: randomized order of dexamphetamine 0.15 mg/kg per dose and methylphenidate 0.3 mg/kg per dose, twice daily for 2 weeks each, 24-hour washout, identical opaque capsules, with investigators, families, children and teachers blind; there was no placebo condition.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Procedure, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Before any medicine, parents reported irritability in 102 children (82%), anxiousness in 96 (77%), daydreams in 94 (75%), proneness to crying in 87 (70%), sadness/unhappiness in 85 (68%), trouble sleeping in 67 (54%) and poor appetite in 43 (34%).
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Discussion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Across the 17 items, the mean number of complaints was 8.19 at baseline, 7.64 on dexamphetamine and 7.19 on methylphenidate (only baseline vs methylphenidate significant), and did not differ between the two drugs; the mean severity of the complaints reported was 4.08, 3.73 and 3.24 (baseline vs methylphenidate and dexamphetamine vs methylphenidate significant).
key_findings.locator: Results › Total Side Effects: Prevalence and Severity, 1st paragraph (p. 663); Table 1 (p. 664)

key_findings.finding: Only two complaints were reported more often on a drug than before treatment: poor appetite on both drugs (59% on dexamphetamine and 56% on methylphenidate, against 34% at baseline) and trouble sleeping on dexamphetamine (70% against 54%; 64% on methylphenidate, not significant against baseline).
key_findings.locator: Results › Individual Side Effects: Prevalence, 3rd paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Compared with baseline, trouble sleeping (mean 3.61 vs 2.21) and poor appetite (2.74 vs 1.22) were rated more severe on dexamphetamine, and only poor appetite (2.12 vs 1.22) on methylphenidate; eight other items were rated less severe on methylphenidate than at baseline and five on dexamphetamine. (Numbers confirmed; 'increased'/'lowered' replaced: these are before-after contrasts without placebo, and the source reports higher ratings at baseline, not that the drugs lowered them.)
key_findings.locator: Results › Individual Side Effects: Severity, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 664); Table 3 (p. 665)

key_findings.finding: Six items were rated more severe on dexamphetamine than on methylphenidate: trouble sleeping (3.61 vs 2.69), irritability (3.65 vs 2.94), proneness to crying (3.4 vs 2.7), anxiousness (2.71 vs 2.07), sadness/unhappiness (2.43 vs 1.69) and nightmares (.79 vs .48); no item was rated more severe on methylphenidate.
key_findings.locator: Results › Individual Side Effects: Severity, 2nd paragraph (p. 664); Table 3 (p. 665)

key_findings.finding: Four children (3.2%) stopped a trial period because of severe adverse effects, two on each drug (1.6% each). On dexamphetamine, an 8-year-old boy became overfocused, extra sensitive and increasingly anxious, and another 8-year-old boy agitated and uncharacteristically aggressive; both tolerated methylphenidate without problems. On methylphenidate, an 11-year-old girl had severe headaches soon after each dose and stopped after 4 days, and a 5-year-old boy became extremely aggressive and tearful; neither had major side effects on dexamphetamine. Each effect resolved immediately when the drug was stopped.
key_findings.locator: Results › Individual Side Effects: Severity, 3rd paragraph (left column, continuing at the top of the right column)

key_findings.finding: Parents rated most children as improved overall compared with their usual selves: 86 (68.8%) on dexamphetamine and 90 (72%) on methylphenidate; beyond a statement, without figures, that teacher and parent Conners ratings generally corroborated these proportions, the paper does not report efficacy, and it does not test this difference.
key_findings.locator: Results › Sample Characteristics, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Severity ratings were generally in the mild range of the 0-to-9 scale. The authors set the 1.6% per drug who could not tolerate it beside 3.6% and 1.9% in two earlier placebo-controlled methylphenidate trials, and cite Ahmann et al.: side effects also fell from baseline on placebo, so comparison with baseline may understate a drug's adverse effects; they add that this would not affect the comparison of the two drugs with each other.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors offer three explanations for complaints reported before treatment that fell on medication: parents seeking a diagnosis may have over-reported at baseline; the complaints may belong to ADHD itself and lessen with treatment; or mothers' globally negative view of a child with difficult behaviour may change once behaviour improves.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors attribute the extra insomnia on dexamphetamine to its longer half-life, and state that only moderate doses given twice a day were studied, that other doses and spacing might change the side-effect profiles, and that no child was younger than 5.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph (p. 665); Discussion, 10th paragraph (p. 666)

reporting_issues.issue: 101 children of mixed type are printed as 81.8%, and the three subtype percentages as printed add up to 101% (Results › Sample Characteristics, 1st paragraph). Editors' arithmetic: 101/125 is 80.8%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; the count (101) and the other two percentages fit n = 125.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says nightmares, stomachaches and anxiousness became less frequent on methylphenidate than at baseline, but Table 2 marks the baseline-versus-methylphenidate contrast for headaches (41% to 24%), not stomachaches (45% to 32%, unmarked); Table 3 likewise shows a significant contrast for headaches and none for stomachaches (p = .16).
reporting_issues.consequence: The word stomachaches in the text appears to be an error for headaches; claims should follow the tables.

reporting_issues.issue: Tables 1 and 3 report F statistics with 2 and 122 degrees of freedom, and neither a missing child nor the handling of the four periods stopped early is mentioned. Editors' inference: for a repeated-measures test across three conditions with Hotelling's test these degrees of freedom imply 124 children analysed, while 125 were enrolled (p. 663).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for the results, but the analysed sample is not fully accounted for.

reporting_issues.issue: Three methylphenidate percentages in Table 2 are one point higher than their counts allow: trouble sleeping 79 (printed 64%), poor appetite 69 (printed 56%), sadness/unhappiness 69 (printed 56%). Editors' arithmetic: with n = 125 these are 63.2%, 55.2% and 55.2%, and no single denominator fits every row.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; claims should use the counts.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says only trouble sleeping and irritability averaged above 3, both on dexamphetamine, but Table 3 also shows proneness to crying at 3.4 on dexamphetamine.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor understatement of the severity of emotional complaints on dexamphetamine.

reporting_issues.issue: Headaches are marked as a significant baseline-versus-methylphenidate contrast in Table 3 although the F test for headaches is printed as p = .01, while significance was defined as p < .01.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headache contrast is borderline and should be treated as uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 gives item means without SDs or confidence intervals, and Table 2 shows no between-drug contrasts, so the size and precision of the six dexamphetamine-versus-methylphenidate differences cannot be computed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims can give the means and the stated significance (p < .01), not effect sizes.

design_detail: Systematic review and frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42021295352; protocol published) of double-blind randomized trials lasting at least 1 week of oral ADHD medicines given alone (amphetamines, lisdexamfetamine as a separate node, atomoxetine, bupropion, clonidine, guanfacine, methylphenidate, modafinil, viloxazine) against each other or placebo. Primary outcomes: change in systolic and diastolic blood pressure (mm Hg) and pulse (beats per minute) at the time closest to 12 weeks; ECG measures secondary. 102 trials: 61 in children and adolescents (13,315 participants) and 41 in adults (9387); median duration 7 weeks. The searches extend those of Cortese et al. (2018) from April 2017 to January 2024. Version of record (the corrected version of 29 May 2025).
can_establish: Average short-term (median 7 weeks) changes in blood pressure and pulse with each ADHD medicine compared with placebo and with each other in double-blind trials, separately for children and adolescents and for adults, with a certainty rating for most estimates.
cannot_establish: Long-term effects on blood pressure or heart rate (4 trials at 24 weeks, none longer); risks of heart disease, stroke, arrhythmia or death (not outcomes); how many people have large rises (aggregate data only; outlier analyses only in the appendix); effects in people with heart disease or at doses above licensed ranges; trial-based comparisons between medicines in adults (all adult trials were placebo-controlled).

sample.recruitment: Searches of BIOSIS Previews, CINAHL, Cochrane CENTRAL, Embase, ERIC, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, PubMed, OpenGrey, Web of Science Core Collection, ProQuest Dissertations and Theses and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform including ClinicalTrials.gov, from inception to 18 January 2024, without language or publication-date restriction; FDA, EMA and manufacturers' websites and the references of reviews and guidelines searched; authors and manufacturers contacted (p. 357). The original searches to 7 April 2017 (9948 records, as described by Cortese et al., 2018) and the updated searches (4752 records) gave 81 and 21 trials (Figure 1, p. 357).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Double-blind randomized trials in children and adolescents (5 to 17 years) or adults with a primary DSM (III to 5-TR) or ICD diagnosis of ADHD or hyperkinetic disorder; oral monotherapy for at least 1 week against another medicine or placebo; FDA-approved medicines within the maximum doses recommended by the most used guidelines, unlicensed medicines at any dose (p. 357).
sample.demographics: Children and adolescents: mean age 11 (SD 3); of available data 73% male and 27% female, 2% Asian, 15% Black, 71% White. Adults: mean age 35 (SD 11); 57% male and 43% female, 6% Asian, 6% Black, 79% White (p. 360). All but four trials recruited exclusively or mainly in high-income countries (p. 360).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; all but two trials contributed short-term data (p. 360).
sample.selection_effects: Short trials (median 7 weeks, IQR 5 to 9); 85% industry funded; sexual, racial and ethnic minorities probably under-represented and results by sex rarely available (pp. 360, 364). Whether people with cardiovascular disease could take part in the trials is not reported in the article; the authors say people with a personal or family history of it might have larger increases (p. 364).

exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Oral; licensed medicines within maximum recommended doses, unlicensed ones at any dose (p. 357). Sensitivity analyses restricted licensed medicines to FDA-licensed doses (p. 359). Amphetamines and lisdexamfetamine were separate nodes, combined in a further sensitivity analysis.

comparison.controls: Placebo or another medicine within trials. Children and adolescents: some head-to-head trials and a connected network (for blood pressure, 1 trial of amphetamines against methylphenidate and 3 of lisdexamfetamine against methylphenidate; for pulse, none of amphetamines against methylphenidate). Adults: only placebo-controlled trials, so every comparison between medicines is indirect (Figure 2, p. 358; pp. 360–361).
comparison.matching: Not applicable (randomized trials). Transitivity was examined by comparing study year, sample size, mean age, proportion of males, sponsorship and risk of bias across comparisons (appendix pp. 12–17, not read) (pp. 358–359).

outcomes.instruments: Systolic and diastolic blood pressure (mm Hg) and pulse (beats per minute), primary; ECG heart rate, PR interval, QRS complex and heart-rate-corrected QT interval (QTc), secondary; rates of outlier values for blood pressure and pulse as defined in each trial, post hoc (pp. 357–358).
outcomes.validity_norms: How the trials measured blood pressure and pulse is not described in the article. Risk of bias assessed with RoB 2 and certainty with CINeMA (high, moderate, low, very low) (p. 359).
outcomes.operationalization: Mean difference (QTc: standardized mean difference) against placebo or between medicines at the time closest to 12 weeks; endpoint values preferred over change from baseline when both were reported (p. 358).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (7 outcomes plus 3 post hoc outlier outcomes, two age groups, every pairwise comparison).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level; the included trials were double-blind. Screening, full-text assessment and extraction were done by two independent researchers (p. 357).

analysis.effect_sizes: Against placebo (mean difference, 95% CI, CINeMA certainty), children and adolescents: methylphenidate systolic 1.81 (1.05 to 2.57, moderate), diastolic 2.42 (1.69 to 3.15, low), pulse 3.88 (2.87 to 4.89 in Figure 3, 4.8 in the text and Figure 5; moderate); amphetamines 0.87 (−0.3 to 2.03), 1.93 (0.74 to 3.11, high), 1.78 (−0.12 to 3.69); lisdexamfetamine 1.76 (0.68 to 2.83, moderate), 2.29 (1.25 to 3.34, low), 4.17 (2.74 to 5.61, very low). Adults: methylphenidate 1.66 (0.38 to 2.93), 1.6 (0.29 to 2.91), 4.37 (3.16 to 5.59); amphetamines 2.3 (0.66 to 3.94), 1.91 (0.17 to 3.65), 5.18 (3.47 to 6.89); lisdexamfetamine 1.62 (−0.81 to 4.06), 3.07 (0.69 to 5.45), 5.07 (2.76 to 7.37); all adult estimates very low certainty. Between medicines, direction as printed (column medicine against row medicine): systolic amphetamines against methylphenidate −0.94 (−2.33 to 0.44, high) in children and adolescents and 0.64 (−1.44 to 2.72) in adults; diastolic methylphenidate against amphetamines 0.49 (−0.88 to 1.87, high) and −0.31 (−2.49 to 1.87); pulse amphetamines against methylphenidate −2.1 (−4.25 to 0.06) and 0.81 (−1.29 to 2.90); systolic lisdexamfetamine against methylphenidate −0.06 (−1.17 to 1.06, moderate) and −0.04 (−2.79 to 2.71); diastolic methylphenidate against lisdexamfetamine 0.13 (−0.98 to 1.24, moderate) and −1.47 (−4.19 to 1.25); pulse lisdexamfetamine against methylphenidate 0.29 (−1.24 to 1.83, low) and 0.69 (−1.92 to 3.3). None of these differences between the stimulants is significant. Heterogeneity was low or low-to-moderate for most outcomes in children and adolescents and moderate or moderate-to-high for most in adults; incoherence could not be assessed in adults (no closed loops).
analysis.covariates: None at review level. Sensitivity analyses: (1) licensed medicines at FDA maximum doses plus unlicensed medicines at any dose; (2) licensed medicines at FDA maximum doses only; (3) QTc by Fridericia or Bazett correction; (4) amphetamines and lisdexamfetamine as one node (p. 359). Their results are only in the appendix (pp. 354–355) and are described by direction in the text (p. 362).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42021295352; protocol published (BMJ Open 2022, reference 15) (p. 357). Outlier rates are labelled post hoc outcomes (p. 358); any other deviation is not described in the article.
analysis.selective_reporting: Medium-term results, outlier rates, ECG comparisons between medicines, sensitivity analyses, heterogeneity and incoherence statistics, risk-of-bias domains and funnel plots are only in the appendix, which was not read. The text's summary of pulse comparisons between medicines leaves out significant differences shown in Figure 5 (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not stated; the authors note that clonidine had only two trials with 189 children and adolescents (p. 364).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Over a median of 7 weeks, methylphenidate, amphetamines and lisdexamfetamine raised average blood pressure by about 1 to 3 mm Hg and pulse by about 2 to 5 beats per minute compared with placebo (the effects of amphetamines on systolic pressure and pulse in children and adolescents were not significant). Methylphenidate, amphetamines and lisdexamfetamine did not differ significantly from each other in either age group. Certainty was mostly moderate to low in children and adolescents and very low in adults.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Discussion describe the average effects as relatively small and warn that individuals may have larger changes (pp. 355, 363–364), which matches the data. Gaps: (1) the Results text says there were no statistically significant pulse differences between medications other than atomoxetine against methylphenidate and viloxazine (p. 362), but Figure 5 marks as significant amphetamines against atomoxetine (−3.8 beats per minute) and against lisdexamfetamine (−2.39) in children and adolescents (p. 361); (2) the abstract's list and ranges of medicines that raised blood pressure or pulse leave out bupropion, which raised adult systolic pressure (3.72) and pulse (2.95) (pp. 355, 359, 361); (3) the Discussion's statement that ADHD medicines have direct effects on cardiovascular safety (p. 363) refers to short-term average changes in blood pressure, pulse and ECG measures, not to cardiovascular events, which were not studied.

timeline.event: Cortese et al. network meta-analysis of efficacy and tolerability, by this review's account the only earlier network meta-analysis with a cardiovascular outcome (blood pressure only) (p. 357); its searches to April 2017 form part of this review's evidence
Protocol published (Lannes et al., BMJ Open; reference 15 of the review; not read)
This network meta-analysis (search to January 2024), with a linked Comment in the same issue (p. 319; not read)

replication.where_it_stands: By its authors' account the first network meta-analysis of a range of cardiovascular measures with ADHD medicines (p. 356). It shares searches, data and authors with Cortese et al. (2018), so the two are not independent. For amphetamines against methylphenidate it shows no significant short-term difference in blood pressure or pulse; adult comparisons are indirect and of very low certainty, and trials say nothing beyond 24 weeks.

what_would_settle_it: Randomized trials or target-trial-emulation cohorts following people for years on an amphetamine or methylphenidate at licensed doses, reporting the distribution of changes (how many people cross clinical thresholds for raised blood pressure or heart rate) and cardiovascular events, including head-to-head comparisons in adults.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Populations, medicines, comparators, outcomes and timepoints specified (pp. 357–358).

domains.domain: 2. Protocol registered before the review (critical)
domains.note: PROSPERO CRD42021295352 and a published protocol (p. 357). Outlier outcomes are labelled post hoc, but the article does not say whether there were other deviations from the protocol or justify them.

domains.domain: 3. Explanation of study designs included
domains.note: Only double-blind randomized trials, chosen because observational studies do not allow causal inference about the drugs' effects (pp. 356–357).

domains.domain: 4. Comprehensive literature search (critical)
domains.note: 12 databases and registries without language or date restriction, regulators' and manufacturers' websites, reference lists and contact with authors and manufacturers; search to January 2024, published April 2025 (pp. 355, 357).

domains.domain: 5. Study selection in duplicate
domains.note: Titles and abstracts screened and full texts assessed by two independent researchers (p. 357).

domains.domain: 6. Data extraction in duplicate
domains.note: Extraction by two independent researchers, disagreements resolved with a senior member of the team (p. 357).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The list of excluded records with reasons is stated to be in the appendix (pp. 20–290) (pp. 357, 360); the appendix was not read, so the item is recorded as no information (METHODS §5.3) and the overall rating stays provisional until it is read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Aggregate description in the article (trials by medicine and age group, ages, sex, ethnicity, duration, countries, funding); study-level characteristics only in the appendix (pp. 330–338), not read.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: RoB 2 for every trial; 81 of 102 at low risk or some concerns, domain-level results in the appendix (pp. 359–360).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Funding of the trials was extracted and reported: 87 of 102 industry funded (p. 360).

domains.domain: 11. Appropriate statistical methods for meta-analysis (critical)
domains.note: Random-effects pairwise and network meta-analyses with a common heterogeneity parameter; incoherence assessed globally (design-by-treatment interaction) and locally (node splitting); transitivity examined (pp. 358–359).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis of the effect of risk of bias on the estimates (no restriction to trials at low risk); risk of bias enters only the CINeMA certainty ratings.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: CINeMA certainty is attached to the estimates and discussed, for example the weak evidence behind the ECG findings (pp. 359–363).

domains.domain: 14. Heterogeneity explained and discussed
domains.note: Heterogeneity and incoherence reported by outcome (p. 362); dose sensitivity analyses address one source; the authors state that aggregate data did not allow moderators to be identified (p. 364).

domains.domain: 15. Publication bias investigated (critical)
domains.note: Contour-enhanced funnel plots for comparisons with more than ten trials did not indicate small-study effects (pp. 359, 362); unpublished data were sought from sponsors and regulators because most trials were industry sponsored (p. 364).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding, the funders' role and the authors' interests are declared (pp. 359, 364).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No critical item is unmet (items 4, 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15 met; item 2 partly met) and one non-critical item is not met (12), which by AMSTAR 2 gives high confidence in the review's conduct. That is not high certainty in its estimates: by the review's own CINeMA ratings most adult estimates are of very low certainty, and every adult comparison between medicines is indirect. Cite for: short-term average changes in blood pressure and pulse with methylphenidate, amphetamines and lisdexamfetamine against placebo and against each other, by age group, with their certainty. Do not cite for: long-term effects, cardiovascular events, the proportion of people with large rises, or effects in people with heart disease.

key_findings.finding: 102 double-blind randomized trials: 61 in children and adolescents (13,315 participants, mean age 11) and 41 in adults (9387, mean age 35); median duration 7 weeks (IQR 5 to 9); 87 (85%) industry funded; 81 (79%) at low risk of bias or some concerns; all but four from high-income countries.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Children and adolescents, compared with placebo: methylphenidate raised systolic blood pressure by 1.81 mm Hg (1.05 to 2.57, moderate certainty), diastolic by 2.42 (1.69 to 3.15, low) and pulse by 3.88 beats per minute (2.87 to 4.89, moderate); lisdexamfetamine by 1.76 (0.68 to 2.83), 2.29 (1.25 to 3.34) and 4.17 (2.74 to 5.61); amphetamines raised diastolic pressure by 1.93 (0.74 to 3.11, high), while their effects on systolic pressure (0.87, −0.3 to 2.03) and pulse (1.78, −0.12 to 3.69) were not significant.
key_findings.locator: Figure 3A
key_findings.note: The upper limit of methylphenidate's pulse effect is 4.89 in Figure 3 but 4.8 in the text (p. 362) and Figure 5 (p. 361); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Adults, compared with placebo: methylphenidate systolic 1.66 mm Hg (0.38 to 2.93), diastolic 1.6 (0.29 to 2.91), pulse 4.37 beats per minute (3.16 to 5.59); amphetamines 2.3 (0.66 to 3.94), 1.91 (0.17 to 3.65), 5.18 (3.47 to 6.89); lisdexamfetamine 1.62 (−0.81 to 4.06, not significant), 3.07 (0.69 to 5.45), 5.07 (2.76 to 7.37); all of very low certainty.
key_findings.locator: Figure 3B; Results, 5th to 7th paragraphs (pp. 361–362)

key_findings.finding: Amphetamines against methylphenidate showed no significant difference: systolic pressure −0.94 mm Hg (−2.33 to 0.44, high certainty) in children and adolescents and 0.64 (−1.44 to 2.72) in adults (amphetamines minus methylphenidate); diastolic 0.49 (−0.88 to 1.87, high) and −0.31 (−2.49 to 1.87) (methylphenidate minus amphetamines, as printed); pulse −2.1 beats per minute (−4.25 to 0.06) and 0.81 (−1.29 to 2.90) (amphetamines minus methylphenidate).

key_findings.note: Signs follow the figures' rule (the medicine defining the column against the medicine defining the row). No CINeMA symbol is printed for the adult cells or for the pulse cell in children and adolescents.

key_findings.finding: Lisdexamfetamine against methylphenidate showed no significant difference: systolic −0.06 mm Hg (−1.17 to 1.06, moderate) in children and adolescents and −0.04 (−2.79 to 2.71) in adults; diastolic 0.13 (−0.98 to 1.24, moderate) and −1.47 (−4.19 to 1.25) (methylphenidate minus lisdexamfetamine, as printed); pulse 0.29 beats per minute (−1.24 to 1.83, low) and 0.69 (−1.92 to 3.3).
