key_findings.finding: The text reports no significant differences between medications in rises of systolic or diastolic pressure in either age group; for pulse, atomoxetine raised it more than methylphenidate (1.70, 0.48 to 2.92, low) and viloxazine (2.79, 0.83 to 4.76, moderate) in children and adolescents. Figure 5 also marks pulse with amphetamines as lower than with atomoxetine (−3.8, −5.91 to −1.68, high) and lower than with lisdexamfetamine (−2.39, −4.78 to −0.01, low) in children and adolescents.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th to 7th paragraphs; Figure 5 (p. 361)

key_findings.finding: In children and adolescents some trials compared medicines directly (for blood pressure, 1 trial of amphetamines against methylphenidate and 3 of lisdexamfetamine against methylphenidate); in adults all trials were placebo-controlled, so the networks were star shaped, every comparison between medicines is indirect, and incoherence could not be assessed.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2, panels A and C (p. 358); Results, 4th paragraph (p. 360, continuing on p. 361); Results, 10th paragraph (p. 362)

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity analyses: when licensed medicines were restricted to their licensed ranges, only amphetamines or lisdexamfetamine were consistently associated with higher blood pressure than placebo in adults; the increases with atomoxetine or methylphenidate in adults were no longer seen, which the authors suggest may indicate dose dependency. Grouping amphetamines with lisdexamfetamine did not change interpretations. The numbers are only in the appendix (pp 354–55, as printed).
key_findings.locator: Results, 11th paragraph (p. 362); Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 363)

key_findings.finding: Post hoc outlier analyses: compared with placebo, amphetamines had higher rates of outlier pulse values in children and adolescents; lisdexamfetamine of outlier diastolic pressure and pulse in children and adolescents; methylphenidate of outlier systolic and diastolic pressure in children and adolescents and of outlier pulse in both age groups. Outliers were defined by each trial, and the numbers are only in the appendix (pp. 356–363).
key_findings.locator: Results, 12th paragraph (p. 362, continuing on p. 363)

key_findings.finding: Only four trials gave medium-term (24-week) results, reported in the appendix, and no trial reported long-term results.
key_findings.locator: Summary, Findings (p. 355); Results, 12th paragraph, end (p. 363)

key_findings.finding: ECG measures against placebo: amphetamines raised ECG heart rate in adults (6.95, 1.98 to 11.92) and shortened the PR interval in children and adolescents (−2.8 ms, −5.09 to −0.51); methylphenidate raised ECG heart rate (3.21, 0.76 to 5.65) and shortened the QRS complex (−1.48, −2.9 to −0.07) in children and adolescents and lengthened it in adults (4.3, 0.92 to 7.68, from one study at unlicensed doses); lisdexamfetamine raised ECG heart rate (4.63, 1.35 to 7.92) and QRS (1.78, 0.01 to 3.55) in children and adolescents. No medicine changed QTc in children and adolescents; in adults atomoxetine raised it (SMD 0.27).
key_findings.locator: Figure 3 (p. 359); Results, 8th and 9th paragraphs (p. 362); Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 363)

key_findings.finding: Contour-enhanced funnel plots did not indicate small-study effects. Heterogeneity was low or low-to-moderate for all outcomes but QTc and heart rate in children and adolescents, and moderate or moderate-to-high for all but PR interval and QRS in adults; in children and adolescents there was local incoherence for systolic and diastolic pressure (2 [17%] of 12 comparisons each), pulse (4 [40%] of 10) and QTc (3 [33%] of 9).
key_findings.locator: Results, 10th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that average effects are generally small but individual patients may have larger changes, and that blood pressure and pulse should be monitored before and during treatment with any ADHD medicine, not stimulants only; they note that aggregate data could not show who is at higher risk.
key_findings.locator: Summary, Interpretation (p. 355); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 363); Discussion, 7th and 8th paragraphs (p. 364)

reporting_issues.issue: The Results text states that, apart from atomoxetine against methylphenidate and viloxazine in children and adolescents, there were no statistically significant differences between medications in pulse increases (p. 362); Figure 5 prints in bold, the mark for an interval excluding no difference, amphetamines against atomoxetine (−3.8, −5.91 to −1.68) and amphetamines against lisdexamfetamine (−2.39, −4.78 to −0.01), as well as modafinil against atomoxetine, lisdexamfetamine and methylphenidate, in children and adolescents (p. 361).
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should follow Figure 5. Among the stimulants, it shows lisdexamfetamine raising pulse more than the other amphetamines in children and adolescents, with low certainty and an interval reaching almost zero.

reporting_issues.issue: The upper confidence limit of methylphenidate's pulse effect in children and adolescents is 4.89 in Figure 3 but 4.8 in the text and in Figure 5.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; 4.89 would round to 4.9, so one of the two values is a misprint.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract lists amphetamines, atomoxetine, lisdexamfetamine, methylphenidate and viloxazine as raising haemodynamic values and gives ranges among them, leaving out bupropion, which raised systolic pressure (3.72, 0.05 to 7.4) and pulse (2.95, 0.08 to 5.81) in adults according to the Results and Figure 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's adult ranges are not the full range of significant effects.

reporting_issues.issue: Several cells of Figures 4 and 5 carry no CINeMA certainty symbol, including every adult cell comparing amphetamines or lisdexamfetamine with methylphenidate, although the legends assign one of four certainty ratings.
reporting_issues.consequence: The certainty of these comparisons cannot be taken from the article.
